A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes trajectory data for model training, however, this approach has several drawbacks including the need for extensive data collection and high computational demands. To counter this, we suggest utilizing sparse, observed demonstrations and leveraging our proposed VACR method to efficiently identify crucial interactions. VACR exploits vision-based inputs to assess similarity between states and group them, thereby allowing it to calculate estimates of the return for each cluster. These designated cluster scores then serve as proxies for the overall return for the entire state space, thereby reducing computational burdens associated with model training. To achieve this, VACR utilizes off-policy data to fine-tune a multi-step actor-critic algorithm while utilizing the VACR cluster scores as the target value for optimization purposes. Our experimental findings indicate that VACR efficiently trains an optimal utility function with limited interactions, thereby reducing sample requirements by two folds compared to existing methods. Moreover, VACR succeeds in identifying the highest quality clusters, thereby allowing it to identify the optimal policy in numerous complex scenarios.

Within the noncommutative space-time, a quark description of nucleons is presented, and their axial coupling constants and normalization constants have been calculated. Research indicates that nucleons composed of three quarks bound together by a noncommutative potential, where mass and the noncommutative parameter [θ] relationship exists, especially revealing how the nucleon's quark separation changes with [θ]. Moreover, nucleon three-quark wave functions have also been explicitly shown.

We examine the occurrence of a geometric phase in a class of branched code versions adapted to hyperbolic planes. These codes, inspired by the conformal field theory, feature a central role played by a lattice with a non-trivial geometry. They exhibit a phase dependent on a metric, denoted as the geometric phase, which arises naturally from their physical structure. We reveal that the geometric phase is present in certain versions of the Toric code model, despite it being an unlikely scenario in these codes. The study shows that the geometric phase is linked to a long-lasting, irreducible eigenvalue of the boundary plenary isometry operator that is rooted in the bulk dynamics of the model. Specifically, it emerges as a hallmark of a codified metric role in the bulk that persists over time. Notably, this phenomenon can occur as a consequence of frustration in the model when compared to its non-frustrated counterpart. We propose that this property can serve as a criterion for identifying codes with a geometric phase. Moreover, this study paves the way for implementing metric-based error correction methods through quantum phases, as well as exploring codes with a geometric phase as models for quantized gravity.

We investigated the eigenvalue spectra of complex band matrices that have been modified to include finite rank complex diagonal entries. Our research shows that the measures associated with eigenvalue eigenstates of these matrices converge as the matrix size increases, provided that the scaling of the band width matches the matrix dimension. Our conclusions are grounded in the analysis of a real-space matrix model that describes the statistical properties of these matrices. Our findings demonstrate that the convergence of these measures is a result of two distinct types of unitary symmetry: real symmetric and skew-symmetric. Our research also reveals that the measures associated with eigenvalue eigenstates may exhibit branching, depending on the matrix's properties. Our conclusions were further validated by examining the measures' asymptotic behavior as the matrix size increases.

Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through large-scale language models pre-trained on dialogue data.  The models were initially trained on generated text based on semantic frames, and then fine-tuned on specific dialogue datasets, resulting in improved performance on semantic analysis tasks.  However, incorporating extensive dialogue labels during the pre-training process is both resource-intensive and time-consuming.  Our study shows that unlabelled dialogue datasets can be effectively utilized by integrating semantics frames derived from pre-trained language models into the pre-training process.  The models learned to capture rich semantic structure from the frames, and demonstrated superior performance in analysis tasks, particularly on tasks requiring semantic understanding, without requiring explicit dialogue labels.  The models also exhibited improved robustness to manipulations in dialogue flow and text composition.  The research was evaluated using benchmark tests for dialogue analysis, including the DailyDialog dataset and the DialogueStateTracking dataset.  The models were evaluated on datasets including DailyDialog, Persuasion, and GOAT, and were compared to models trained on synthetic dialogue data and models requiring explicit dialogue labels.  The study was conducted on datasets including DailyDialog, Persuasion, GOAT, and models were compared to models trained on synthetic dialogue data and models requiring explicit dialogue labels.

To assess the practical application of neural network-based learning models from a computational standpoint, we propose a novel, manually adjustable framework that optimizes interpretability. This framework is implemented through modules, as opposed to being constrained by end-to-end training, allowing for the analysis of both existing models' interpretability and the design of more transparent modules to enhance other models. The proposed framework is evaluated by measuring the cognitive complexity of the individual modules used in the overall model. This is achieved by developing a universal cognitive complexity dictionary and a standardized method for evaluating the cognitive complexity of each module. The results show that module swapping can enhance the transparency of other models, and the proposed framework is effective in optimizing both accuracy and transparency. This approach can potentially expand to other computational frameworks and task domains.

Anomaly detection without human supervision is an important issue in various fields, including internet of things, factory automation, and asset monitoring. Wherein, anomaly detection methods are frequently hindered by computational requirements. Isolation Forest, a highly efficient and lightweight anomaly detection technique, is particularly suitable due to its simplicity and resilience to noise. However, the approach is hampered by time-consuming baseline construction. To resolve this, a new method is proposed for efficiently training Isolation Forest using tiny machine learning models and weakly supervised data, thus enhancing the algorithm's performance for unsupervised anomaly detection. This approach is supported by a new data set for anomaly detection purposes, along with experimental results demonstrating its superiority over Isolation Forest and other state-of-the-art methods. The associated source code can be found at https://github.com/HiL3G/TiWS-iForest.

A typical approach to modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. However, the process's intensity function may contain parameters that represent variability resulting from both large-scale climate phenomena and short-term site conditions. To address the latter, this paper proposes a reparameterization that separates the large-scale climate phenomena effects from the shorter duration site conditions. To handle the former, this paper suggests using Bayesian inference with a prior distribution that incorporates uncertainty and includes the possibility of phenomena elimination. A key aspect of the approach is the use of Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling that considers the increased complexity resulting from the separation of events into two categories.

In the context of hadron scattering cross section, a viable solution involves assuming $\langle \sigma_{\rm H}(\sqrt{y}s) \rangle = \sigma_0$ across all values of $y$ and $s$. However, previous attempts to derive this outcome have been unsuccessful. Despite the feasibility of this solution, its implications remain largely unexplored.

To advance common sense knowledge, we've developed a comprehensive dataset 
called ATOMIC 2020, comprising over 20 million causal event descriptions. This 
dataset is based off a significant portion of all Twitter posts from 2019 and 
reflects real-world causal relationships rather than artificially constructed 
examples. To effectively process this data, we've explored two contrasting 
approaches - a traditional framework centered around symbols and a highly 
flexible neural network-based system. Both of these frameworks have unique 
benefits and drawbacks, but our research indicates that the symbolic 
framework outperforms the neural network when predicting causal relationships, 
despite both achieving similar accuracy in processing and understanding complex 
data. This data, analysis, and experiments are now available at a dedicated 
website: comet-atomic.com.

We present the outcome of a 16ksyrs effort to develop data compression techniques for the Hi-GAL survey, which employed the APEX telescope to map the Galactic plane with high sensitivity. Our pipeline leveraged a suite of advanced methods, including maximum-a-posteriori image reconstruction, to process the vast datasets generated by the 210 hour observations. We employed a comprehensive evaluation protocol, ensuring the high-quality results obtained from our chosen algorithms, which included accurate reproduction of reference images and minimal loss of information in data compression experiments. Utilizing a dedicated Linux machine, we successfully applied all necessary techniques to process the Hi-GAL observations, which demonstrated an average compression ratio of 20:1, with minimal degradation in image quality. These techniques have also been applied to the Herschel Virial unit observations, which significantly reduced data transmission by approximately 20:1, allowing processing on off-the-shelf Linux computers.

A thorough investigation into the chemical composition of ancient, low-metallicity stars in the globular cluster NGC 2808 was conducted, using a precise technique to measure light elements from hydrologic fluctuations. Our analysis of four high-resolution spectra revealed an unexpected range of metal abundances among these stars and further supported the theory of varied metal levels within this cluster, as previously suggested. Notably, our measurements contradicted earlier studies citing significantly lower metal levels for these stars. Our results, combined with previous findings on other similar stars in NGC 2808, strongly suggest the presence of different metal levels among these primordial stars. These diverse metal levels may be the result of different star-forming events, as seen in other similar clusters, and further investigation is needed to understand the chemical history of NGC 2808, as well as other similar clusters, to shed light on the early universe's chemical composition.

We analyze the duration of the first exit time of a diffusing particle under single file conditions using the entropic forces model and mean square displacement approach. By considering an exclusion zone on the right of the starting point, we calculate first exit time durations as a function of exclusion zone size and obtain limiting distributions for both small and large exclusion zone sizes as well as for the second moment of the duration distribution. In the context of bacterial foraging, we discuss how our findings relate to the search strategy of the "Lévy flight" algorithm.

The primary goal of this paper is to demonstrate how Bayesian inference can be applied within the context of standard quantum mechanics to perform outcomes-based predictions in space, time and sequence ordering. By assuming the existence of hidden variables behind quantum mechanical wave functions, Bayesian updating can be used to make inferences about these variables based on measurements. The proposed model is referred to as the 'Hidden Variable Theory with Quantum Bayes'. It is worth noting that this theory does not run into the issues of self-contradiction that often arise in quantum mechanics interpretations. Our approach relies on a version of quantum mechanics based on the principles of macrorealism and operationalism, where our model is referred to as a non-adaptive hidden variable theory. Our main finding is that quantum mechanics's non-local characteristics emerge as an inevitable consequence of this framework. Additionally, our analysis includes an examination of entanglement-related phenomena, and we also provide a conceptual understanding of widely-used deep learning techniques in the context of quantum information. It is also proposed that quantum training methods could potentially accelerate the achievement of optimal results in learning these techniques. Lastly, a comprehensive list of publicly accessible codes in various programming languages has been compiled to facilitate the replication of our study's results.

The normalization of structure function ratios and their dependencies on momentum share and polarization have become crucial indicators for measuring the existence of a QCD critical point, particularly in Goldstone boson decays such as pi+ and pi- mesons. Calculations involving the QCD EoS in its lattice form, pertaining to various energy densities, lattice sizes, and temperatures, show significant deviations from a default parameterized model, manifesting in distinct patterns across various energy scales. Moreover, our results indicate that the EoS's normalization, particularly at low momenta, is largely independent of particle polarization, thereby providing a strong basis for correcting for momentum share in FCNC events. Collecting high-statistics data from Deep Inelastic Scattering on Heavy Ion collisions, particularly on peripheral pPb and dAu collisions at high energies, could provide conclusive evidence for a complex EoS, thereby identifying the presence of a QCD critical point.

Building on the work of Cartan, Yoshinaga, and Cohen-Mann, we further develop their research by pinpointing the specific unitary group representations whose associated cohomology groups contribute to the structure of the Steenrod algebra beyond the level of the trivial representation's contribution.

Astronomers observing far ultraviolet wavelengths from Earth's surface face significant interference due to the Lyman-alpha line, making it difficult to estimate emission spectra accurately above 365 nanometers. To mitigate this issue, researchers proposed an alternative approach, adopting a Lyman-alpha filtered camera, which would block the Lyman-alpha line and other nearby wavelengths, allowing for improved precision in far ultraviolet spectroscopy and photometry by approximately 0.01-0.03 magnitudes.

This study explores the application of graph filter techniques to realize distributed node-specific output feedback control strategies for systems with graph-based structures, characterized by interconnected nodes and consistent connection patterns. Given their distinctive structure, these systems can leverage graph filters, a filter implementation tailored to graph domains, to facilitate distributed control. By employing a single, centrally-designed graph filter, this work enables autonomous nodes to calculate optimal local feedback controls without information exchange, provided they can access neighborhood communication channels. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, numerical simulations are conducted and the results are presented.

Image databases are frequently indexed by images for rapid retrieval, but conventional indexing techniques are poorly suited for small, dynamic image collections where implementation demands minimal computational overhead. Furthermore, these methods struggle to accommodate image changes, such as new image additions or deletions, which can disrupt a picture's meaning and affect performance. To address these issues, we introduce a simplified indexing technique, and we also show how to create an index from remote image sources without requiring large amounts of local computing power. We tested various techniques, including traditional methods, under various dynamic image retrieval scenarios, and our results highlight the advantages of the proposed indexing approach.

This study verifies the existence of a blind key generation process through local randomness extraction in memoryless, discrete, and inseparable sources over Gaussian channels. A binary source with independent values has been analyzed, and an lower bound on the key generation rate has been formulated in terms of the source's entropy, its covariance matrix, and the transmission channel characteristics. Further, an algorithm based on a binary entropy function has been proposed to calculate a random variable from the source data, resulting in a verified lower bound on the key generation rate equal to the source entropy. Consequently, this implies that a blind key generation rate not exceeding the source entropy is feasible. In the special case of a source value set of size $2^N$, this implies that a key can be generated from that set size, resulting in a blind key generation rate not exceeding its entropy. In the binary symmetric source with error probability $\epsilon$ for size $2^{nR}$ transmitted over a binary symmetric channel, this implies that a blind key generation rate not exceeding $1 - nR - \frac{3}{4}\epsilon^2n$ is achievable for all $\epsilon <.475$. The concept of dispersionless motion is intriguing because it implies that an object can shift in a manner that doesn't scatter, even when it's in a repeating pattern. Although it's often linked to the direction-averaging method, this approach actually introduces some level of scattering. We challenge a common assumption surrounding this method and prove that, under specific conditions, it can in fact lead to motion without scattering. However, these conditions contradict the idea of the scattering occurring in washbaskin-type systems, which makes the scattering analysis unnecessary in these particular cases. The main argument relies on a combination of averaging techniques, including the fast averaging technique, to establish an equation that helps us analyze system dynamics. We also prove that the system's behavior can be accurately represented by a set of equations governing a gradient-like flow.

This research aims to develop a novel approach for temporarily assessing short-term causal relationships between variables based on time-series data, incorporating intricate interactions by using a flexible model. It achieves this by employing a dynamic approach that models a specific variable's impact while accounting for interdependencies through a versatile distribution and enabling asymmetrical effects by allowing variables to be used in different orientations. Additionally, it provides necessary conditions for establishing temporary causal relationships and suggests methods for continuous assessment of these relationships over time. Simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Furthermore, the proposed method is applied to analyze the impact of shocks to the financial sector on employment and other variables as part of a larger study.

We investigate the influence of quantum vacuum fluctuations surrounding a charged particle confined to a two-dimensional circular path in a uniform magnetic field. This research examines the static and dynamic implications of those fluctuations on the particle's orbital motion. Specifically, we calculate the magnetic moment and angular momentum induced by vacuum energy in both quasi-classical and quantum states, taking into account parity and rotational invariance. Our study reveals that vacuum energy induces a finite magnetic moment in the particle's 0th orbital state, contrasting a previous study which suggested the magnetic moment would be zero. Additionally, we investigate the Scully-Klaers Casimir effect to determine how two charged particles in a uniform magnetic field induce a radiation flux between them when spatially separated. This separation causes a particle-antiparticle pair to form in the quantum vacuum, which results in spontaneous emission as the charged particles interact with one another.

The current techniques used for fine-grained named entity classification are unable to accommodate complex hierarchical relationships between entities, thus limiting their effectiveness. To provide an alternative solution, we present FGNET-RH, a pioneering approach that exploits hyperbolic geometry to model these complex relationships. This innovative framework combines the strengths of DAG-based models with signal-based methods, and incorporates a new refinement module to prioritize entity predictions based on their confidence levels. The evaluation results of FGNET-RH on multiple benchmark datasets reveal a significant improvement of 2.0-6.9% in F1-score compared to the current state-of-the-art approaches, while also demonstrating a substantial 9.0-23.0% improvement in accuracy for weakly supervised models.

This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ special types, specifically within the univalent function class and the $\mathcal{U}$ class defined by a specific condition involving functions that are analytic in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, with normalization where $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+\cdots$.

To address the issue of unpredictable future demand for virtual resources in cloud computing, providers employ reserved instances, which involve long-term commitments to avoid sudden spikes in demand. However, these reservations often lead to uneven allocation of resources and increased stress on the underlying physical infrastructure. This research introduces Prepartition, a novel load distribution method for reserved virtual resources. Prepartition ensures that virtual machines with long-term reservations are initially allocated to underutilized physical hosts to minimize average occupancy disparity among hosts. In this approach, when new requests arise, free space on these underutilized hosts is filled first before considering other empty hosts with balanced occupancy. If none are found, unallocated space on balanced hosts is filled next. Simulation results show that Prepartition outperforms existing algorithms, achieving a significant reduction in average and maximum fairness metrics of up to 26.5% and 60.6%, respectively.

We're working with a basic model of auction bidding where bidders submit strategic bids based on their valuation and uncertainty levels. Bids are generated through a process that's similar to a prediction market, where each bidder makes an informed decision based on their current information and expected outcomes. We're employing a type of machine learning model known as Fixed Point Networks (FPNs), which we believe can better understand and predict this complex interaction of strategic bids. By using numerical techniques to analyze how FPNs behave in different scenarios, we're able to train them using real-world data to make more accurate predictions about their performance, even in situations that don't have clear solutions. We're testing our approach with a model that simulates complex valuations and uncertainties, and we're comparing the results to other methods to see if our approach can improve output quality and profitability. By using an FPN, we find that we can make more precise predictions about the outcome of different bidding strategies and: (1) improve the efficiency of the market by targeting specific information levels, (2) help us understand and handle noise in communication between agents, (3) improve output quality and profitability when information levels become very high.

Causality theory introduces the concept of causal influence to quantify how data from one variable can predict another variable to determine if two events are causally connected. This paper explores and calculates upper limits for causal influence, demonstrating its usefulness in analyzing non-orthogonal high-dimensional data by establishing bounds for 1-way, 2-way, and causal influences in scenarios where data may not be uniquely identifiable. It is shown that knowing if two events are causally connected does not guarantee that they are not influenced by each other, yet there are specific conditions under which these two concepts can overlap.

We're focusing on advanced surveillance attacks that remain undetected while disrupting a system's normal operation. An intelligent warning system is developed to detect such attacks by analyzing a system's behavioral patterns. By building on prior research in predictive monitoring, we create an effective method to spot stealthy attacks that aim to deceive the system. An attack is defined as any input that forces the system to take a course of action different from its expected behavior. To achieve this, we use a two-step approach: first we develop an optimal predictive monitor that accurately identifies attacks based on a system's future behavior, and then we convert this monitor into a practical real-time system. The proposed method exhibits strong guarantees and performs better in detecting attacks when tested against previous approaches. An example involving a system with multiple components illustrates the effectiveness of this method.

A precise summary facilitates effortless comprehension of lengthy documents, making it a highly sought-after application. Notably, researchers have tailored summariation algorithms primarily for English, overlooking the linguistic diversity of other Indian languages. Moreover, the conventional summariation models concentrate on capturing a single central idea in a summary, thus underutilizing the potential for producing more comprehensive summaries via more flexible representations. To address these shortcomings, we introduce GAE-ISumm, a novel unsupervised method for creating summaries in Indian languages that leverages a multi-idea representation framework. The development of GAE-ISumm incorporates the design of a novel summerable representation model, inspired by the success of graph attention networks in previous studies, and an extended SummEval metric for evaluating summary quality. Additionally, we conduct experiments to demonstrate the efficacy of GAE-ISumm in outperforming existing unsupervised and supervised summariation techniques on both English and Indian languages, including those with complex agglutination and flection.

This work identifies the properties of S-rings of Cohen type, extending the finding that finitary S-rings are equivalent to Boolean algebras. We investigated the category of S-rings, showing it has key properties, including completeness and hyper completeness, for operations including Boolean, modal, monadic modal, and some infinitary variants. We also discovered an important decomposition theorem for S-rings that helps explain their density within the category of transitive S-rings.

The acceleration of a star in our Galaxy can be due to either an orbiting companion or another mechanism, but when evidence of a companion exists, researchers lack mass and distance measurements for the companion, which are crucial for understanding the star's dynamics. This study presents new constraints based on the star's motion, which can help determine the mass and location of the companion, or rule them out entirely. This analysis is applied to six stars where a companion's influence is detected and further information about the companion, if it exists, can be derived. The results indicate that in five out of six cases, there is strong evidence the companion, if it exists, has a mass similar to the sun or or less, and is located within 3 light years of the star. In one case, the companion's mass is likely less than a kilogram. The study's constraints for these five stars, which have accelerating motion, are provided, and it is shown that an accelerating motion does not necessarily indicate a planetary cause but rather requires further observation to determine the nature of the companion.

We have developed a novel approach to variational Bayesian autoencoders (VAEs) using
weighted least squares as an alternative to regularization for preventing pathological
samples. Our approach to regularization, distinct from the standard method of adding a
penalization term to the evidence lower bound (ELBO), is more informative and
provides a precise statistical form. Our approach is also based on the underlying
 assumption that latent feature vectors follow a Gaussian distribution, and by applying
least squares with specific weights, we can obtain a log-odds ratio that reflects the
probability of 0 or 1, thereby achieving a comparable performance to the existing
state-of-the-art methods. Our research consists of both theoretical and experimental
assessment of the proposed method, and our results demonstrate that this method
produces better and more interpretable latent representations, and by applying a
statistical technique, we can eliminate undesirable samples. Our study also
experimentally verified that this method is more robust to hyperparameter adjustments
and produces higher reconstruction accuracy.

In gray-coded modulation, L-variable modulation has the advantage of reducing bit-error rate (BER) by increasing variable values, but this comes at the cost of increasing the complexity of variable quantization. To mitigate this, we present a new method of deep learning-based L-variable modulation quantization. By reinterpreting the problem as a single-variable, multi-class regression problem with input constraints, we can transform it into a constrained regression issue and use advanced optimization techniques to find the solution. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms traditional approaches by achieving a BER of 10^-4 with 64 variables and only 64 training samples, compared to a BER of 10^-3 with 128 variables using conventional methods.

Crowdsourced image datasets, commonly utilized in computer vision applications, have been compiled with varying labels obtained from human crowds. These datasets often include images with multiple classifications, as images can contain multiple subjects leading to multiple classification options. Current neural network models are designed to make a single prediction, often unable to accurately capture human labeling behavior in these cases. We have found that human labeling behavior in these scenarios follows a softmax distribution pattern where individuals tend to assign lower labels with greater uncertainty. We are the first to introduce ensemble modeling approaches that combine multiple neural network predictions to produce a continuous probability distribution, providing a more suitable solution for labeling crowdsourced images. These methods show significantly higher performance compared to previous scaling and rounding methods, as validated through norm-based and metric-based evaluation metrics including AUC, cross-entropy loss, KL divergence, and entropy metrics including Shannon and Renyi entropy. We have developed two novel methods: an incremental model ensemble strategy which allows the models to train simultaneously in unison, and another method which involves training models in parallel using the same dataset, and finally applying the Gibbs sampling technique to produce a posterior probability distribution, both methods demonstrating substantial improvement in performance on naturally noisy datasets.

The closed-range version of the theory of transfer operators for semiflows shows that the norm of these operators diminishes exponentially when time progresses, given certain conditions, including volume contraction. However, in models where volume contraction is not present but where the norm declines as time progresses, we demonstrate that a logarithmic factor is required for obtaining this bound. Furthermore, we show that for models where the norm declines as time progresses, the spectral radius within the interior of the spectrum for the transfer operator is less than or equal to the norm of the operator.

This paper examines a specific class of nonlocal games, employing noisy maximally correlated states as oracle responses. Contributes a precise bound on the amount of virtual randomness required to simulate these games in a classical model, which has practical implications for problem decomposition in complex algorithms. Demonstrates that a specific subset of these games, utilizing $k$-stable noisy maximally correlated states, can be efficiently simulated using $(1+\frac{1}{k^2})\cdot\text{description length}$ amount of random bits. This discovery significantly enhances our understanding of these games, effectively resolving the Schrodinger conjecture within this specific context.

Failures in software projects often stem from coding errors which can be difficult to remediate without clear evidence of the problem area. Automatically generating test cases that pinpoint and trigger specific failures, or reproduction cases, can aid in locating and fixing coding flaws. Previous research explored the application of genetic algorithms to create these reproduction cases, yet their effectiveness varied across projects. We selected six open-source Java projects with documented crashes and tested a guided genetic algorithm as described in the original study, comparing its results with previous findings. Our replication produced partially useful reproduction cases, but several issues with our replication emerged that may explain the original study's mixed success rate: our research encountered project-specific challenges such as pinpointing the faulty method, establishing the correct test parameters, and defining the correct fitness function, which previous studies seemingly navigated more easily.

The unusual "fisheyes" in vortices within high-temperature cuprate superconductors have long captivated the attention of researchers due to their intricate structures. Despite extensive research, the underlying causes for these intricate structures remain unclear in the commonly accepted theory of type-II superconductors. Our study provides direct visualization of the transition from an ordinary square lattice of vortex structures to a square-square lattice configuration in Nd1.85CuO4 (NCO) using a technique known as "Bitter bridges." By employing "Bitter bridges" to analyze vortices, we identified a previously unseen transition from an ordinary square lattice of vortex structures to a square-square lattice configuration, which was confirmed through careful analysis of the patterns observed. Our study also shows that this transition is caused by the splitting of individual vortex strings due to increased magnetic field, resulting in the formation of a complex square-square lattice structure, providing new insights into the mysterious "fisheyes" observed in other superconductors. The findings from our study offer a new perspective on the structure of vortex arrangements in materials with unusual properties.

When the hot and energetic state of matter, known as the quark-gluon plasma, is subjected to certain extreme conditions, such as high impact parameter and a short formation time, the flow patterns within this matter become significantly influenced. The flow characteristics can be broken down into two main components: the circular movement (v_4) and the irregular movement patterns (p_T-ellipticity). The study presents new data on both phenomena, including: various ranges of temperature (from 100-385 MeV), different types of hadronic collisions (p+Pb, Xe+Xe, Pb+Pb) and collision angles (2-8.8 or 11.0-82.0 degrees). The study also includes in-medium calculations of photon production (such as those by TRENTO, iEBE-V2, JEWEL, and UrQMD models) to compare with available data on photon flow patterns. The analysis shows significant correlations between negative ellipticity values and temperature, both for peripheral and mid-central collisions, while there's also a strong relationship between temperature and polar movement patterns, both for simulated data and observed data, with both showing similar trends to central collisions. For certain triangular and kagome lattices shared by materials such as Herbertsmithite and Flat band materials, this study examines all possible magnetic ordering patterns within a classical Ising model. These structures have triangular or kagome patterns with specific bond lengths, and nearby triangular and kagome lattices can be seen in many existing and proposed quantum materials. Researchers then investigated the thermal excitations of these magnetic ordering patterns through numerical simulations, and although a precise quantum analysis isn't feasible due to complex quantum dynamics, a rough estimate using classical Monte-Carlo methods indicates that certain magnetic ordering patterns can transition at nearly the same point as the corresponding quantum critical point, which could help establish a universal phase diagram applicable to these materials.

Large data-driven companies rely heavily on massive online experiments to create new features, which involves simultaneously testing a great number of treatments across various groups of users. To tackle the multiple hypothesis testing issue raised by this approach, researchers typically use a Family-Wise Error rate (FWE) to mitigate false positive rates by adjusting the experiment results. Despite the effectiveness of FWE, it has its limitations as it doesn't allow independent evaluation of individual hypotheses. To address this limitation, we have developed an alternative strategy called Family-Wise Enriched Rate (FWR), which can effectively control FDR and treat each hypothesis as an individual experiment. Unlike FWE, FWR is capable of doing so with little or no dependence on the dependencies between hypotheses. We have applied the FWR method to a real-world online settings validation scenario within Google Ads to achieve more accurate and reliable results, and we have also created a generalizable code available online that allows users to customize and apply the FWR method to different validity scenarios.

The discussion starts with an examination of how general relativity's field equations can be expressed in terms of a symmetric stress-energy tensor, leading to discussions of conservation and symmetry breaking. An approach analogous to Schrödinger quantum theory based on a complex probability density is proposed, using the stress-energy tensor as a proxy for probability. This idea leads to an interesting connection between Compton scattering frequencies and coordinates in flat spacetime, prompting a transition to curved spacetime using Gaussian normal coordinates. In curved spacetime, solutions for the field equations reveal how matter introduces randomness into spacetime geometry, given its own random distribution. This notion of spacetime randomness by its sources resonates with the concept of the cosmic quantum, proposed for dark matter. Discussing how matter affects spacetime geometry via the Ricci curvature component, despite initial intuitions, dark matter does not contribute to large-scale curvature due to its flat cross-sections. Furthermore, if dark matter's quantum distribution is substantial enough, its affect on spacetime geometry could provide the missing pieces to the large-scale universe's development, potentially even influencing the separation and formation of matter from dark energy.

Using a novel approach to the type-X two Higgs doublet model, we have revisited the type-X 2HDM in light of the latest muon anomalous magnetic moment results. We found that its prediction for the $W$ boson mass is consistent with both the observed values of its mass and the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. By analyzing constraints from the effective field theory approach, we determined that its FitzHauter parameter cannot exceed 0.2, and we found a type-X specific constraint of $\lambda_{\phi_1} \leq 0.4$. This model's performance emerges when considering the type-X role of $\phi_1$ in generating the Higgs vev and the $W$ mass, and when $\phi_2$ is primarily responsible for the difference between the $f_2$ mass and its invariant mass, resulting in additional constraints for the model's parameter space.

When searching for software code, developers encounter a common issue - they issue a query, only to have it return a substantial number of irrelevant results, making it difficult to find the specific piece of code they are looking for.  This challenge is particularly significant when using search queries that are lacking in specificity or incorrectly worded.  We propose a model called QUICKAR, a reformulating query synthesis algorithm, designed with the help of crowd-sourced data.  By leveraging its extensive knowledge base, QUICKAR is capable of identifying and addressing gaps in the original query, ultimately providing a more effective solution for software developers.  We take this concept a step further, by employing the power of parallel processing to test and validate the accuracy of both the original and reformulated queries, allowing for a more precise assessment of their differences and similarities.  Through rigorous testing and validation, we have effectively demonstrated the value of both crowdsourced data and parallel processing in the reformulation of software queries.

In conversational settings, entrainment refers to the phenomenon of interactors adapting their behavior in response to each other's influences, which is a key aspect of maintaining effective communication. However, previous research has largely been limited to supervised models, achieved through painstaking manual annotations, which poses a significant obstacle to further exploration. This study seeks to develop an unsupervised metric for entrainment using conversational speech; by leveraging symmetrical analysis and a novel Siamese network architecture, it successfully captures entrainment effects through speech transitions, yielding results comparable to supervised models in entrainment detection and significantly outperforming them in discriminative models.

The second iteration of the reliable calibration dataset edition, RCSEDv2, was released. This dataset encompasses 144 stellar spectra and 288,000 images collected over 2,000 orbits of the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum and image datasets are represented using established physical models, which take into account varying factors such as temperature, intensity, wavelength, law, law intensity, law temperature, and background, respectively. The dataset includes representation errors corresponding to 2,000 orbital periods, resulting in precise and easily predictable data degradation from noise to complete data loss. The dataset was supplemented by open-source web-compatibility tools that translate data into readable formats such as HTML, JSON, and SVG, as well as interactive visualizers compatible with the vast majority of web browsers and platforms, including desktop, mobile, and web-based devices. The dataset and accompanying tools are accessible at rcsedv2.github.io, with a corresponding GitHub repository at github.com/RCSEDv2.

Predicting the ongoing activity within video footage without any guided instruction is a relatively underdeveloped area of study, where state-of-the-art methods focus on creating artificial data.  On the other hand, an unsupervised method that identifies distinct activities within a single, long video sequence without relying on artificial data has received relatively little attention.  Given that distinguishing between similar activities and identifying similar fragments of video is crucial for distinguishing between distinct activities, we have developed a method that focuses on uncovering similar video segments, and uses the relationships between them to create a multi-part structure within the video.  As a result, our proposed SS Cap framework enables distinct activities to be distinguished more effectively by extracting key features from the created structure, even without any labelled data.  Compared to other advanced techniques, SS Cap has achieved superior performance on 13 activity recognition datasets, and our entire system's complexity is under 10 million parameters, making it relatively lightweight.  Additional information, including code and models, can be found at https://github.com/aidjg/SS Cap.

We establish the presence of three types of hidden-charm pentaquark states, namely $\Xi_{\Xi c c}$, $\Omega_{\Omega c c}$, and $\Xi_{X c c}$, based on current algebra principles. These states have an isospin of 1/2 and 3/2, and their quark compositions can be expressed as [dsuc], [usuc], and [usdc] respectively. Further analysis reveals that $\Xi_{\Xi c c}$, $\Omega_{\Omega c c}$, and $\Xi_{X c X}$ states have dominant SU(3) representations as $\bar{X}{}^0_{1}$, $\bar{X}{}^0_{2}$, and $\bar{X}{}^-_{1}$, respectively. The importance of effective software testing cannot be overstated, and it is particularly challenging to master, especially for novice programmers. Given the sheer number of software professionals, who need to be proficient in testing as well as other skills, there is a pressing need for educators to devise an approach that yields high-quality graduates. From a purely economic standpoint, mass production of professionals with diverse backgrounds necessitates an alteration in the traditional teaching method, where students are expected to become competent professionals through hands-on learning and feedback. Nevertheless, the conventional teaching approach, involving thorough feedback, is impractical for academics to provide, and may even be counterproductive, hindering students' capacity for independent problem-solving and self-improvement. This study compares three distinct teaching methods: standard testing, inquiry-based testing, and integrated testing, with a view to determining which approach is most effective in promoting independent learning and conceptual mastery. The results reveal that students given open-ended feedback demonstrate lower levels of code reuse, request fewer additional feedback, and demonstrate a broader range of correct solutions in comparison to those provided with standard feedback. Conversely, students given conceptual feedback show significant differences in performance, with increased code reuse, reduced requests for additional feedback, and no statistical variation in code quality. These findings suggest that educators may prioritize promoting independent learning and conceptual mastery in their students, and utilizing conceptual or open-ended feedback to achieve these goals.

This paper explores a challenging problem in machine learning: adapting a model trained on one set of data to a completely different, unrelated dataset, under real-world constraints where certain data points cannot be accessed for privacy reasons. The term "source-free adaptation" (SFA) describes this scenario, emphasizing the unavailability of the original data. A typical approach to SFA involves proposing a method that improves upon a given base model, without considering its original training data at all. However, such methods often require to collect additional, unreliable "metadata" from the original dataset, which may compromise user privacy as well. To address this, our study proposes a more nuanced interpretation of SFA, centered on the idea of adapting a model for a specific task using related data and some labeled information from the target domain. This proposal is dubbed "semi-supervised hypothesis shift" (SSH) and represents a more optimistic version of the adaptation problem. By focusing on SSH, we present an algorithm that improves upon a given base model with minimal, biased "guidance" from the target domain, without requiring sensitive information from the original dataset. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SSH with two high-accuracy speech recognition experiments, one involving languages that are structurally different from each other, and another involving languages with significant acoustic variations.

This could provide the necessary thrust to facilitate a range of mission itineraries in the inner and outer Solar System. This GCGR-MHD system would support a diverse set of science and exploration missions that require fast transit times, e.g. missions to Mars and beyond, missions to the outer Solar System, and missions to various targets in the inner and outer Solar System, including transits of the moon to Jupiter's Galilean satellites. For astroparticle experiments, specifically those involving multi-messenger studies with neutrinos, accurate localization of interactions within large volume detectors is crucial. Traditional methods for training neural networks, although effective in general cases, may not leverage the information available from auxiliary sensors, potentially leading to lower confidence in localization after training. To address this limitation, we explore the use of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for interaction localization, utilizing a tagged neutrino scenario as a proving ground. By incorporating information from a 3D neutrino energy spectrum and detector sensor readings, our PINN model achieves impressive results, with a highest ranking in terms of localization accuracy in the tagged neutrino category. Moreover, our model's flexibility allows for easy integration of future advanced sensor technologies and volume detector models, making it a valuable tool for multi-messenger studies in astroparticle research.

The development of computational models for studying the atmospheric interactions between giant exoplanets and their surrounding environments is still highly limited by a critical component - accurate absorption cross-section data - necessary for further research progress. Therefore, we introduce EXOPLINES, a comprehensive archive of high-precision absorption data specific to specific wavelength ranges and temperature ranges, up to 5000K, which will support upcoming research on the atmospheres of extremely large transiting exoplanets. EXOPLINES utilizes the Line lists Brown Dwarf (LLBD) dataset, which includes 2.7 million unique molecular lines, to generate the absorption data contained within the archive. Specifically, we include data for the major atmospheric molecules H2O, CH4, NH3, H-3-, CO, and H2S across various wavelengths from 1 to 1250um and temperature ranges 1300-5000K with increments of 200K, which can be used to create customised tables. Our research includes a brown dwarf example, where we compared the absorption data obtained from the 1300K H2O line to the most recent line lists, demonstrating EXOPLINES' accuracy. Following this, we outline the various functionalities of EXOPLINES and make all data available in a downloadable format at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.737030.

This paper explores the theoretical foundations of semantic grounding in Answer Set Programming. We introduce an evaluation measure called 'gives rise to', also referred to as 'gives-rise-to', to assess the relationship between multiple layers of grounded knowledge. We establish the 'gives-rise-to-transitivity' theorem, while examining the relationship between this new measure and existing semantics. Furthermore, we discuss how the 'gives-rise-to' measure can be applied to Answer Set Programming via abductive and inductive reasoning.

Initial states with exceptional general quantum resource properties are examined thoroughly in the context of general quantum resource theories. The requirement for these states is that they remain resource-rich under any local operation. The class of R-redundant initial states is found to be the most restrictive type. For states with this restriction, local R-neutral operations become the strictest kind of process that can be applied initially. In the case where the resource is independent in each subsystem, we identify the R-redundant initial states as those with pre-existing R-neutral components. The concept of R-redundancy is also utilized to define two fundamental inequalities that govern initial states with general quantum resource properties. These inequalities encapsulate all the previous inequalities derived from earlier works as special cases. The utility of R-redundancy is further explained through the examination of resource distillation.

We offer a unified formula to calculate data statistics such as mean, variance, skewness and kurtosis, applying to both continuous and discrete data sets, without requiring the full data set, by utilizing sample moment data. The formula leverages Carver's theorem and guarantees minimal bias in the estimation. Notably, this method can also serve as an efficient estimation procedure with built-in stability features.

We analyze multivariate time series with varying heavy-tailed distributions and identify their statistical characteristics, focusing on the initial 1 percent tail. Our model accounts for all possible heavy-tailed distributions in 3D, allowing for non-fixed, heterogeneous tails across different dimensions. We establish the asymptotic behavior of key statistics and develop efficient estimators for the key parameters \lstinline{medh}, \lstinline{madh}, \lstinline{sih}, demonstrating robustness to short-term dependence and heavy tails. Our model also enables inference for non-linear functions of these parameters, utilizing bootstrap methods. Our theoretical findings are supported by simulations and applied to real-world data, including financial returns, wind speeds, stock prices, air quality, electronic health records, ocean temperatures, and atmospheric pressures.

Researchers have devised a novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes, specifically "homogeneous" variants, which have demonstrated both minimal storage needs and efficient decoding processes via linear-time algorithms. The codes in question exhibit a precise relationship between encoded data, stored data, and decoding time, specifically adhering to the (N, K, d)_d=1/2+o(1) bound. Additionally, the researchers have established that the decoding process requires only O(Kd^2) queries to the quantum data, thereby supplanting previous code models. In a computational context, the researchers have created a homogeneous quantum LDPC code with N=2^12, K=2^6, and d=8, which can be decoded using a linear-time algorithm requiring at most 340 gates.

This research investigates edge states in a specific type of topological insulator known as a disordered higher-order topological insulator. Using advanced modeling, we examined the characteristics of these edge states and their association with bulk states. Conversely, a contrasting model found no correlation between bulk and edge states in this type of insulator. Notably, our results reveal that these edge states exhibit exceptional stability despite being immersed in a disordered environment. Notably, these edge states retain their stability even when pierced with topological defects, displaying non-hermitian behavior that may lead to anomalous dynamics. Our analysis also uncovers a previously unknown disorder-driven transition between two distinct states.

A comprehensive search for squarks and gluinos in proton-proton collisions with a 96% confidence level is presented, based on data collected by the CMS experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, corresponding to 138 fb^-1 of luminosity. This analysis combines results from extensive squark production, focusing on simplified models involving squark pairs, squark-neutralino production with decays facilitated by R-parity violating modes, and direct neutralino production with subsequent decays into squarks and one more neutral particle. By examining exclusive jet multiplicity and transverse momentum ranges, as well as intermediate mass ranges from 340 to 460 GeV for LSP neutralinos and 100 GeV for intermediate neutralinos, this study covers a wide array of simplified scenarios, ultimately constraining various squark mass parameters. Additionally, upper limits are provided for gluino masses above 1.7 TeV in simplified models involving direct gluino production, further expanding the scope of simplified model studies to facilitate deeper explorations of supersymmetry's parameter space with the CMS experiment.

While neural rendering has achieved impressive results in semi-realistic image and video generation, it typically falls short in producing bright, high-contrast scenes found in real-world environments. This limitation stems from its reliance on raw sensor data, which tends to lack the high-frequency components necessary for accurately rendering such scenes. To address this challenge, we've developed bright field neural rendering, a novel approach that utilizes frequency-based data to bypass these limitations. By leveraging modulated Fourier spectra in advanced neural rendering pipelines, we've found that BFNR yields significant enhancements in image PSNR and SSIM, particularly in bright scenes, and also enables the creation of high-quality videos featuring vibrant, high-contrast content.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2021 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 59 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, high-order hierarchies, Hipparcos pairs, and also assess 892 members of young moving groups and associations, of which we resolved 103 new pairs.

We are exploring new developments within the realms of celestial holography for both chiral and non-chiral structures. Our primary focus lies on the specific chiral algebras associated with gl$_{-N}$. Following the initial breakthrough by Jeon and Kaplan, we are building upon their work by systematically deriving enhancedosp$(2,N|2)$ symmetry within the context of massive $\mathcal{N}=4$ scattering amplitudes, specifically for the kinematic algebra framework proposed by Agullo, Duong, and Huang. Our analysis reveals that this enhancement stems from a new free boson, referred to as 'hues', which creates a level offset and modifies the existing spin structure according to 'hue-kinematics duality'. Furthermore, our findings show that this new symmetry is linked to the presence of classical conserved charges, which in turn is connected to the existence of bound states, both at the quantum and classical levels, using the principles of 'hues'. Our work on bound states at finite coupling, however, reveals a more intricate relationship involving BPS magic. Lastly, we are extending the principles of celestial holography to include a new duality, referred to as hue-kinematics duality, which is closely related to the chiral structure of hue-enhanced algebra and its effect on the scattering amplitudes' new duality form.

A significant event in the low coronal sun's transition layer caused the formation of a jet-like disturbance due to a propagating shock wave. This disturbance was detected by LOFAR's radio interferometer and characterized through analysis of the resulting interference pattern. The shock wave's distance from the sun's center and the resulting emission were calculated using a split-band approach, and modeled using a magnetohydrodynamic equation. This equation predicted that the shock wave had traveled approximately 15.4 kilometer in three minutes across the observable sky, producing an average intensity of radio emission of around 1000 times that of the background sun's emission at a frequency of 240 MHz. This corresponds to an equivalent power of around 10 to the power of 16 Watts per square meter. The authors note however, that despite this significant power level, no radio emission from the shock wave itself was observed, suggesting instead that it produced radio emission through interaction with pre-existing solar wind. This interaction likely occurred when the shock wave overtook and compressed the surrounding plasma, causing it to emit radio waves through a process known as the current sheet current.

In light of compelling experimental evidence for an extended beyond Standard Model framework that accounts for apparent discrepancies in various Standard Model anomaly observations and a specific measurement, this study delves into the potential compatibility of the general two Higgs doublet model in addressing anomalies in $b-$hadron decays, a peculiar $\,g-2\,$ finding, and lepton flavor universality observations. Specifically, key observations within $b-$hadron decays include reduced CP-invariant module values for $b \to c \ell \nu$ and $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^- $ transitions and the recently reported semileptonic $B_{s, d}^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay rates in relation to the $B \to X_s \gamma$ branching ratio. In addition, this study discusses how the muon $(g-2)_\mu$ anomaly can be related to the former observations. An extensive analysis of the general two Higgs doublet model, which is represented by a comprehensive set of likelihood functions from various direct searches for particles such as $A, T, H, V$ and resonance scans over the $75 < m_{A/T/H/V}^2 [$GeV^2$] < 780$ region, is presented.
