The Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation, which has previously predicted local extrema of spacetime, now further develops its concepts with the discovery of bipolar outflows acting as a repulsive force of gravity. This prediction stems from an analogy with a liquid having surface tension, where the ejection of mass creates cavities that produce the observed repulsive effect on surrounding spacetime. Based on this theory, we have derived mathematical equations describing this phenomenon, which also led to the discovery of a nonlinear equation for unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable unstable, showcasing its complex dynamics. This phenomenon can be observed in various astrophysical objects, which may serve as evidence to support the theory.

Our research involves an in-depth analysis of various observable patterns that might accompany fast radio bursts, including their potential optical and X-ray emissions. By carefully studying the characteristics of repeating FRBs with known positions, such as repeating FRB 20120904A, we established strict limits on any associated optical or X-ray radiation. These findings serve as significant boundaries for theoretical models that necessitate the presence of externally shining objects or intense optical/ X-ray radiation. Our study also sets new standards for future experiments aiming to detect these rare events. Furthermore, our research reveals that there is no noticeable connection between repeating FRBs and established galaxy clusters or large galaxy clusters. This discovery has important implications for the significant task of identifying the origins of FRBs.

This paper presents an overview of our research on the conceptual design, improvement, and reverse engineering of high-power laser facilities. We report recent advancements in energy transfer, beam expansion, and tuning methods. Additionally, we outline our approach to analyzing and valuing experimental parameters, which has led to the development of predictive models for tuning strategies, beam expansion, and energy distribution. These models enable us to assess the feasibility of achieving specified parameters within given pump energy ranges. Furthermore, our analytical framework allows us to estimate parametric degradation resulting from experimental deviations and serves as a guide for optimizing tuning methods, particularly in tuning strategies, making this process more reliable.

The capability of language models to generate coherent text based on context and learn from observations through reinforcement and supervised learning has been established, but their potential to acquire knowledge from visual inputs remains uncertain. This study demonstrates that language models can be trained to incorporate visual information for text generation in two new tasks. First, we designed the Visual Coherent Captioning task, which requires models to incorporate visual data to create more coherent captions during inference. This allows models to learn to focus on visual elements that impact text generation. Secondly, we developed the Visually Grounded GPT-2 Text Ranking (VGGTRT) task, which enables models to weight visual features for text generation by learning to assign importance to individual visual elements. This study provides new insights into the capacity of language models to utilize visual inputs and advances the development of multimodal language models.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of two core components, namely an encryption technique that conceals transaction details and a confidential addressing system.
The Delegated RingCT scheme comprises two major components: the encryptions of transaction details and stealth addresses.
The Delegated RingCT scheme supports a variety of stealth addresses.
The Delegated RingCT scheme boasts multiple benefits, including the ability to be used in conjunction with various stealth address formats.
The Delegated RingCT scheme offers an adaptable framework that can be used in conjunction with different encryption algorithms for transaction details.
The Delegated RingCT scheme incorporates key benefits, including the ability to incorporate new features in the future.
The Delegated RingCT scheme significantly accelerates transaction confirmation and address creation.
The Delegated RingCT scheme presents a more compact format compared to previous versions.
The Delegated RingCT scheme incorporates a new transaction detail encryption method, known as XTRList.
The Delegated RingCT scheme incorporates a method to estimate the size requirements for transaction detail encryptions, known as XTRList.
Our research indicates that Delegated RingCT provides quick and confidential transaction capabilities for DPOS networks, supporting a range of stealth addresses.

The primary function of an accelerator is to accelerate charged particles up to high energies, with researchers using brightness scans as a tool to investigate how well this task is accomplished.  In the process of accelerating particles, issues can arise, affecting the beam's quality and ultimately its brightness.  To address these problems, researchers employ brightness scans as a means of detecting and understanding beam anomalies, spanning a range from simple issues like beam loading to the complex phenomena of Landau damping.  This paper will provide an overview of brightness scans as a diagnostic tool, with an examination of how they're executed, the data collection process, beam data analysis, and relevant considerations for free-electron lasers.

To address the pressing issue of electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), experts have been working to develop accurate prediction models. However, traditional analytical models are often limited by their reliance on established formulas and available data. A novel, collaborative data-driven approach to EMC modeling is emerging, enabled by powerful computational tools and vast amounts of measurable data. This development allows experts to treat EMC problems as black-box functions, feeding in measurement data to generate predictive models that can accurately navigate complex valleys and peaks. Yet, data-driven models face uncertainty and limitations in their reproducibility, contextual applicability, and ability to generalize. This paper explores the potential of a new collaborative architecture for data-driven EMC models, which can learn from diverse datasets across multiple contexts to develop versatile and adaptable models that predict unknown metrics more accurately than existing standards and traditional models. By harnessing the collective power of data and computational expertise, this innovative approach promises to revolutionize EMC modeling and unlock the full potential of data-driven technology.

This study examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$
state accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles, where $n=1,2,3$. It's assumed
$\Upsilon(10753)$ belongs to a typical bottomonium under the $4S$-$3D$ mixing
scenario. To analyze the decay mechanism, this research computes diagonal decay
amplitudes via a relativistic, effective Hamiltonian, taking into account the
contributions of various charmless resonance intermediaries. Notably, this study
supports the assignment of a $4S$-$3D$ mixing scenario for $\Upsilon(10753)$.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a differential problem with constraints. Then, we derive a differential problem with constraints that incorporates the quantization constraints. A specific class of such problems is defined as interval-restricted problems which have closed intervals as constraints. AskewSGD is a novel algorithm that solves this class of problems. It modifies Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) to iteratively update bounds that minimize excess gradient with respect to the optimized point. Each iteration of AskewSGD corresponds to a single SGD step, making it computationally efficient. We have found that AskewSGD not only converges rapidly, but also accurately determines the optimal point by converging to the theoretical optimal solution in the gradient descent context. We tested AskewSGD on various neural network topologies, data types, and with different quantization schemes. AskewSGD was found to outperform current quantized neural network training algorithms, such as PACT and ZeroQ, in terms of accuracy and training speed.

The ability to control soft robots safely and efficiently in complex unstructured environments is a key advantage of soft robotic systems over traditional rigid robots. However, achieving this goal proves difficult due to the intricate mechanics involved, often necessitating intricate mathematical modeling to grasp the behavior of these robots. This paper offers an in-depth review of cutting-edge research focusing on the model-driven control of soft robotic systems through a comprehensive analysis of the existing literature. It covers key modeling techniques for various systems, control methodologies, and optimization methods used. Additionally, the paper highlights existing challenges and encourages further research in this field.

The Jacobian group of a genus-g transcendence degree algebra is a crucial object with high complexity. It has been studied over the past century by notable mathematicians including Weil, Siegel, Kanai, Oda, Shaferevich, Andre, Zilber, and Poon. Their individual contributions paved the way for subsequent progress. This paper aims to significantally expand our knowledge and provide an updated perspective on certain aspects of the subject.

Confirming large-scale facts poses a significant challenge due to the underdeveloped state of knowledge retrieval capabilities. Current methods rely heavily on text search and often struggle with accuracy and efficiency. In this research, we focus on the fact verification task and introduce an innovative solution that leverages disassembly. By breaking down online content using subject-predicate-object queries and storing the results in structured data frames, we can improve fact verification and related tasks. Our proposed method not only enhances retrieval efficiency but also significantly improves verification accuracy. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions.

While generative adversarial networks effectively generate realistic images for a given condition, there's a crucial requirement to ensure they produce data that is also consistent from a semantic perspective. Notably, conditional GANs translate condition data into a condition space specific to the network, which is then used to train the generator. However, there's no guarantee that this condition space accurately captures the data's underlying semantics. Consequently, when networks are deployed in real-world scenarios, it's unclear what impact the condition space has on image quality, and whether adjustments to condition space representations affect the generated images. To address these questions, we examined two widely used image classification datasets, namely, the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, to analyze how network architectures like ResNet and PreAct Net represent condition spaces when conditioned on image classifications. By measuring the similarity between condition space representations and the corresponding semantic labels, we found that ResNet and PreAct Net condition spaces outperform other state-of-the-art architectures like Caricature Net, which was specifically designed for generating facial caricatures. Notably, when we employed the PCA transform to decode the condition spaces, we discovered that the top principal components accurately reflect the condition (i.e., image classification label) semantics. To further validate these results, a distance metric was proposed for comparing the generated images with actual data. Experiments on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrated that there's a strong correlation between this measure and generated image quality.

The nested sampling method offers a precise alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, computing the posterior probability distribution's normalisation constant without being affected by computational efficiency. Its main drawback is its relatively slow convergence, partly due to the suboptimal exploration of the posterior space, with only a limited number of highly optimistic parameter choices being sampled each iteration. Various methods have been suggested to choose the most optimistic parameter choices, each with their own strengths and limitations. This paper introduces four step acceptance methods for nested sampling, incorporating an adaptive multilevel search, a hit-and-run algorithm, the Monte Carlo Metropolis method, and a sequential metropolis method. These methods are compared with the original nested sampling approach, as well as a sequence-based candidate generator that was previously proposed, on a set of differential equation solving problems.

In various network applications, distance labeling has been used to efficiently compute shortest path distances between multiple pairs of nodes. A significant improvement over single-pair shortest paths was achieved with fault-tolerant distance labeling, allowing the computation of distances after the failure of any node or edge. Building upon this concept, fault-resilient distance labeling considers the computation of shortest path distances between any pair of surviving nodes after the failure of up to k-1 nodes and an arbitrary k-node connectivity-critical subset of edges. In our work, we study fault-resilient distance labeling in weighted planar graphs and propose a labeling scheme that requires significantly fewer bits than previously proposed techniques, while also demonstrating a bit complexity status for d-dimensional graphs.

In this research, we investigate inter and intragroup correlations in pairs of bosons within a forced, dissipative Bose-Hubbard model as a function of time and frequency. The model consists of two groups linked to opposite phases of an oscillating laser field. Correlations between bosons in the same group experience a characteristic drop followed by a rebound, separated by a static interval. Through the calculation of two-player correlation functions over time, our findings reveal an asymmetry based on frequency, explaining fluctuations in boson numbers. By employing a many-body, mean-field approach, our model's phase boundaries, derived from a mean-field Hamiltonian with respect to dissipation, are established and compared to previous studies. Additionally, our work marks the first application of a quantum jump and wave approach to understanding pair correlations in the Bose-Hubbard model.

They had examined a PDE with significant principles within a particular bounded area of $\mathbb{R}^N$. By studying how the equation behaves when the diffusion matrix and vector are relatively regular, they established that a hypothesis related to the equation's left-hand side being close to the right-hand side, in terms of divergence, is a necessary and sufficient condition for a solution to exist. Our study focuses on a more complex scenario where the diffusion matrix and vector have limitations, defined as $Q\in L^\infty$ and $b\in L^2$, respectively. We extend this by introducing additional restrictions where the symmetric part of $b$ and $\mathrm{tr}(Q)$ have antiderivatives within the considered Lebesgue space. By applying specific principles within a particular bounded area of $\mathbb{R}^N$, we establish that a hypothesis related to the equation's left-hand side and right-hand side, in terms of divergence, being close for a current variable, is a necessary and sufficient condition for a solution to exist. Our study also covers a particular variation of $H$ and introduces further restrictions where the divergence of $b$ and $\mathrm{tr}(Q)$ have antiderivatives within the considered Lebesgue space. To identify novel OOD detection methods that don't rely on data-driven approaches, we consider decision boundaries generated by Gaussian Processes. This decision boundary is based on a Gaussian distribution with mean and variance inferred from training data. However, since its covariances don't accurately represent uncertainty, we replace it with a hierarchical group decision strategy. This stratified approach uses different GPs or LAs to analyze data, and a statistical test to determine which group is most representative. This IGCFP method is evaluated on CV, AIChallenge, and UDA datasets, comparing it to existing GPs and other classification methods. Although GPs have higher OOD detection rates than other GPs, IGCFP method performs better in dense domains, surpassing other methods in OOD detection rates. This approach also maintains efficiency, being significantly faster than other GPs.

In a recent study, researchers explored the behavior of a quantum gas in an optically trapped state, exposed to a driven and coupled optical lattice and quasiparticle condensate. The system, powered by a strong laser, exhibited unusual characteristics. The team showed that a specific "scar" state, originally observed in non-driven systems and featuring a unique, discrete spectrum, could support a non-equilibrium quasiparticle condensate. This condensate was found to stem from a "fountain of atoms" that repeatedly interacts with the trap's edges and undergoes cooling. The presence of a local, attractive interaction was found to play a crucial role in this process, ultimately giving rise to Bose-Einstein condensation. The predicted phenomenon is highly controllable and makes the use of both driving and coupling schemes highly appealing for future experiments.

The article demonstrates sharp inequalities for solutions $u$ of the Monge--Amp\`ere equation in $\mathbb R^N$ with a nonnegative boundary value $f$, showing that the difference between the supremum of $u$ over a bounded domain $D$ and the infimum of $u$ over $\mathbb R^N\setminus D$ is bounded by a specific expression in terms of the diameter of $D$ and the value of $f$, or that $u$ is uniformly H\"older continuous with a corresponding bound involving $\mathrm{Diam}(D)$ and $f$.

Counting the recurrence of a periodic event allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a significant endeavor. We will instead examine a "optical clock" that lacks periodicity and operates by counting the occurrence of random photons. This notion serves as an analogy for timekeeping, where the time told will depend on the specific method used to synchronize individual optical clock instances. We discuss the implications of starting these clocks at different points in time and will will draw a parallel to phase measurement based on optical interferometry.

This research proposes an effective network management strategy for fog-based service delivery networks that combine fault prevention, detection, and recovery, and optimize resource utilization for achieving low latency in real-time applications. The proposed method involves automatic fog node selection and QoS guarantee through optimization of service delivery paths, fault detection and prevention mechanisms, and an online network monitoring system for real-time network traffic analysis and failure detection. Upon failure detection, the management system efficiently triggers network restoration and resource reconfiguration to minimize service disruption. Simulation results show that the proposed method reduces service disruption time, and fault prevention significantly decreases the frequency of failures, while fog nodes are efficiently utilized.

Metric learning uses a pair of images and optimizes a distance metric to match similar images closely, with small distances, and large distances for those that differ greatly. Various loss functions have been explored to improve the quality of distance metrics. To gain more insight into these loss functions, we've created 'gradient surgery', which allows us to analyze the evolution of the distance metric and image embeddings during training. Our analysis tool is being used to make connections between images, embeddings, and the distance metric, and to provide a link between training progress and final model performance. Gradient surgery has been used to provide a training progress explanation for low-shot and zero-shot scenarios, and to demonstrate how different loss functions work, and improve their performance.

In this study, we propose a type of Ryans's invariant MERA as a form of approximated holographic error correction code that can be constructed without supervision and is characterized by power-law relationships. We research multiple instances of this code and establish lower bounds on their capacity to withstand errors; these codes can also be looked at as combinations of four different unitary error correction codes that are characterized by distinct power-law relationships. We then use the previously developed quantum multiple valued Shannon theorem to determine the maximum amount of information that can be transmitted through a channel based on the hyper-invariant MERA to determine the maximum amount of information that can be transmitted through a channel based on the hyper-invariant MERA. Additionally, by employing a straightforward encoding method, we show that a channel that was previously difficult to communicate through can become easy when the output is fed into the error correction code, and vice versa for a channel that was previously easy. This research reveals the error correction capabilities of the hyper-invariant MERA and its potential role in advancing our understanding of the relationship between local dynamics and long-distance communication in complex quantum systems.

The researchers studied the structural characteristics of a large-scale filament system centered around the Galactic Center, leveraging a database of 1828^o dust continuum map from the ATLAS^3D Galaxies survey. In a preceding study, they examined the physical properties and density distributions of these filaments using probability density functions and found them to resemble each other closely. In this part of the investigation, they looked into the spacing between the filaments, discovering they vary from approximately 17 to 108 parsecs, with a typical separation of about 32 parsecs, and a power law distribution of separation lengths, with a power of approximately 2.4, with significant variations in the distribution. The average density of the filaments was found to decrease as the distance between them increases, and further analysis using simulation suggests that these filaments are largely self-similar, and the authors propose to describe their large-scale structure as a 3-dimensional network with a fractal dimension of about 2.4, and suggest that this network may play a role in shaping other components surrounding the Galactic Center, including other Galactic Center filaments and star clusters.

This paper presents a new approach for distributed optimization of conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems with interconnected primary and secondary networks. To reduce energy consumption under constraints at substation levels, a novel distributed gradient method is introduced for optimal CVR distribution control. The method proposed relies on a Bilinear Congruence Programming model that is free from matrix noncircuity, allowing it to be solved efficiently with high accuracy by Z-projection. The approach has been tested on a real-world distribution network and compared with other methods, showcasing its efficiency and effectiveness. Furthermore, the method can be extended to various other optimization problems.

This research investigates delayed-arrival bandit problems where the arrival times depend on the chosen arms. We introduce a delay-dependent version of the information-theoretic Regret Framework and apply it to derive lower bounds for general, non-stochastic problems. Moreover, we expand upon a prior work that addressed Bernoulli bandits in the delayed-arrival setting and now addresses general non-stochastic problems. Our solutions for non-stochastic problems outperform those derived from the Regret Framework, often by factors of $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ and $\Omega(n)$. Additionally, we address an advisor setting where an external advisor offers arm choices and demonstrate an algorithm pairing well with the advisor's decisions.

Current text-generation algorithms produce high-quality conversations with humans, yet the conversations often lack the richness and nuance of those initiated by native speakers. To rectify this, our team has developed LEATHER, a groundbreaking framework that teaches machines to initiate conversations with human-like precision. By combining research in natural language, psychology, and computer science, LEATHER empowers the system to make informed decisions about text composition, thereby enhancing its overall message delivery. Through its cutting-edge design, LEATHER opens up fresh avenues for the development of more sophisticated and sophisticated text-producing systems in the future.

Following the groundbreaking confirmation of the existence of quarks and gluons, a profound understanding of the fundamental forces in nature was achieved, yet it also gave rise to three major unsolved puzzles, namely the origin of dark matter, dark energy, and the nature of matter at the onset of the universe, which gave rise to quantum chromodynamics, a theoretical framework describing the interactions between these novel particles, although it proved to be incompatible with certain notions of a fundamental theory due to certain issues, and attempts have been made to reformulate it and incorporate a temporal and spatial component, and despite certain difficulties, quantum chromodynamics has enabled scientists to make precise predictions regarding certain properties of hadrons, and various approximations and numerical methods have been employed to tackle the complexities involved in characterizing thermal and dynamical properties of strongly interacting matter, and in this review, the underlying concepts and methods of lattice regularizations are discussed in the context of quantum chromodynamics, and the discussion is extended to phenomena related to chiral phase transitions, phase diagrams, and exotic states of matter, and the review is concluded with a perspective on potential future developments in the field.

As the demand for accurate wind-turbine stress predictions increases, particularly to minimize costly structural damage, the use of high-fidelity simulations is impractical due to their high computational demands. To overcome this challenge, a more efficient approach is proposed - an innovative probabilistic machine learning method, which frames the uncertainty associated with predictive stresses as a probability distribution. By leveraging Gaussian Processes, this method models the uncertainty associated with random environmental variables and their interactions with uncertain turbine configurations. Two critical components of the model are the prediction of uncertainty associated with stress predictions related to specific turbine configurations, and the estimation of distribution parameters for evaluating the model's reliability. To address these challenges, two novel techniques are introduced - the application of Gaussian Processes in predicting stress uncertainty, and the use of Bayesian inference, respectively. Furthermore, a technique is developed to adapt and learn the distribution parameters of the proposed model, which simulates the interactions among diverse environmental random variables and their impacts on predictive stresses. By simulating the distribution of the leading surrogate model, the method demonstrates its ability to simulate the interaction among diverse environmental random variables and their impacts on predictive stresses. By simulating the leading surrogate model, the method demonstrates its ability to simulate the interaction among diverse environmental random variables and their impacts on predictive stresses. Results from both smooth and noisy inputs indicate that the method accurately captures the underlying uncertainty associated with predictive stresses, which demonstrates its ability to simulate the interaction among diverse environmental random variables and their impacts on predictive stresses. Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake in Turkey, aiming to enable authorities to track real-time public sentiment during crises. We investigate the correlation between derived Linguistic Invariant Variables and the public's emotional response to the earthquake, investigating the impact of linguistic variables on emotional expressions using logistic regression models. We discovered significant linguistic variable derivations indicating the public's emotional response, showcasing the value of such variables in understanding emotional expressions during crises.

A group G holds the property $R_\infty$ if every action of G on an infinite set yields an orbit with infinite stabilizer. We're looking at generalized abelian Baumslag-Solter groups, finding that any of its nilpotent quotients meet the $R_\infty$ criterion, except in cases where those quotients equal $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on a trajectory basis for optimization. This novel framework combines the benefits of trajectory models, offering simplicity and clarity like molecular dynamics, yet can be computed like a neural network, providing fast and efficient processing. Additionally, this approach allows for the processing of data in pairs, offering improved stability and accuracy even with small data sets. It is successfully tested on data from experiments involving molecules to analyze complex chemical reactions, where it is used to develop models that can simulate and predict likely outcomes.

This paper presents SceNDD, a unique naturalistic driving dataset, gathered on a diverse set of trajectories. Unlike other data collected through instrumented traffic, SceNDD was recorded on various routes, resulting in more naturalized driving patterns. The dataset is based on 57 miles of driving, collected by a single driver, who navigated different roads and conditions at different times of day. Unlike other available data, SceNDD doesn't rely on predetermined test routes, allowing it to capture a more authentic driving environment. The dataset is divided into 18 miles of instrumental data, 16 miles of rush hour traffic, and 23 miles of exotic traffic, which was obtained by driving on unfamiliar routes during non-peak hours and non-traffic routes during peak hours, respectively. Rush Hour and Exotic traffic offer a higher level of driving difficulty, Rush Hour being mostly straight and flat, Exotic being mostly curved and luminous. SceNDD is structured to facilitate situation-based driving, featuring seven unique driving scenarios, including following another vehicle, driving alongside another vehicle, driving on a lane dividers, passing another vehicle, changing lanes, stopping, driving ahead of another vehicle. Each situation is annotated manually, offering valuable context for training and testing of driving models. The dataset is complemented by several automated processing techniques, including extraction of relevant data from the OBD II interface, resizing and formatting the video and annotations to standardized formats, and creating interactive tools for visualizing and exploring

This work focuses on the reflected entropy in conformal field theory, specifically considering scenarios where the underlying theory has a boundary or an interface. For both cases, we have demonstrated an identity linking the reflected entropy and the entanglement entropy, thereby confirming the previous findings of Ghosh and Hermon for the boundary scenario and Han and Wu for the interface scenario. Additionally, our derivation yields a generalised version of a formula first discovered by Maloney and Susskind. For the instance scenario, our study also yields two separate identities linking the reflected entropy, entanglement entropy, and the mutual reflection entropy.

Recently, research interest in Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted wireless communication has been consistently growing.
Notably, existing studies on RIS-aided systems often overlook the practical limitations of real-world systems, such as excessive interference due to insufficient guard intervals even with compensation algorithms in place.
In this context, we focus on a specific system utilizing orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) and relying on enhanced extreme learning machine (ELM)-based channel evaluation for mitigating interference.
Our proposed framework combines an elliptic least squares (ELS) method with an advanced ELM framework for optimal system performance.
Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed framework significantly outperforms conventional models by achieving a 90% reduction in bit error rate (BER), with 96% increased energy efficiency further improved by 25% compared to the standard elliptic least squares (ELS) method.

In 1967, Iñiguez established the Integral Variation theorem, which demonstrates that a set of positive operators with a unified spectrum of unity can be represented as a mixture of separate positive operators, each with a unique spectrum. Although originally, no additional conditions were considered, later research found this assertion to be incorrect in projective measurement scenarios. However, it was later proven to be true under the condition of projectivity. Our study shows that the assertion is false in non-projective measurement scenarios well, and we identify necessary and sufficient conditions on the spectral structure that make the assertion valid.

Over almost G_2 manifolds with SU(3) structures, our research shows that deformed G_2 instantons have a straightforward complexification. This involves expanding on earlier work, using connections that slightly deviate from the Levi-Civita connection. This expansion leads to the discovery that the space of deformed instantons is structurally similar to the space of conventional instantons. This similarity implies that deformed instantons exist in abundance and can even be collectively adjusted to zero.

The swift spread of the COVID-19 pandemic has led countries to implement strict control measures to slow its progression, including the mandatory use of contact tracing apps to track infected individuals and curb the outbreak's progression. These contact tracing apps primarily rely on proximity tracking, leveraging radio signal strengths to identify and monitor individuals in close proximity to confirmed COVID-19 cases. As the global shift towards contact tracing apps accelerates, nations are grappling with the challenge of finding a balance between using these systems to combat the pandemic and protecting their citizens' right to privacy. This study focuses on the privacy aspects of contact tracing apps, specifically analyzing the national COVID-19 tracing app used in Brazil and developing a localized variant, Coronavirus-SUS EP, which incorporates features from the European contact tracing apps to enhance user privacy. This study's primary contribution is to evaluate the privacy aspects of the Coronavirus-SUS EP in depth, and to demonstrate the efficacy of the DECO Contact Tracing protocol in preventing unauthorized access to user data, including hackers employed by third parties and infected COVID-19 cases seeking to compromise user privacy by revealing sensitive location data that could potentially spread the virus further.

Recent findings indicate that some behaviors of neural circuits, often referred to as classical models, can also be accurately explained by a quantum emotional memory process. For instance, a memories that doesn't change concept, known as long term potentiation, can be accounted for by a quantum emotional memory process. Furthermore, the short term effects of a brain memory, known as long term potentiation, and memory loss, known as long term forgetting, are also capable of being explained. An investigation was conducted using randomly generated patterns from a normal distribution to see how well different models, including a quantum emotional memory process, could fit these results. An analysis revealed that a quantum emotional memory process is significantly more capable of fitting these results than a classical model.

ACL2 has successfully integrated C through a relatively straightforward process, allowing for the development of complex software and software verification tools that incorporate C components, all within a purely logical ACL2 environment. Building upon this embedded C, our system leverages ACL2's reasoning capabilities to automatically generate C code and corresponding ACL2 theorems for custom applications. The generated C code comes with a guarantee of correctness in the form of accompanying ACL2 theorems. Given its relatively minimal embedding, our C embedded in ACL2 can be treated as a proof-based front-end for C development, enabling the creation of custom C code with automated, theoretically guaranteed correctness.

A notable feature of asteroid spectroscopy is the presence of M-types, which exhibit bright red colors, and less discussed phenomena, such as pure rotational spectroscopic absorption bands caused by molecules. Notably, pure rotational spectroscopic absorption bands are relatively infrequent among asteroids, with only a few potential locations known so far, such as Brucker's lines on Brucus and Iochroma. Iochroma is a unique M-type asteroid with several unique characteristics, and recent studies using CLAY and SpeX have made significant advancements in understanding its composition, but have not captured pure rotational spectroscopic absorption bands, despite the presence of other sources indicating these features could be present. A new study using SpeX data from 0.8 to 2.4 microns has revealed these absorption bands, and analysis using Ueda-Nagataki's equation has matched these bands to ethane at low temperatures, but have also found a discrepancy between calculated and observed phases of 60 degrees, which suggests the presence of other substances because ethane only accounts for 60% of the absorption. Additionally, ethane is not matched with Brucker's numbers which place the bands at 5.0 microns, and this has led researchers to consider other options for interpreting Iochroma's data and its impact on its overall composition.

Ramanujan proposed a formula to express odd zeta values in terms of hyperbolic automorphic functions. This paper reformulates this equation using the Hurwitz zeta function, providing a new representation. Additionally, the article introduces an algorithm to exact zeta values, focusing specifically on the case for zeta(5/2)).

We investigated the elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces constructed from projective V-spaces. These complex projective spaces include elliptic cohomology theories tailored to toroidal actions, generating cohomology classes. We identified specific generators for such theories in terms of cohomology classes in the elliptic cohomology ring. These generators can be represented as the sum of two classes, one of which is fixed under the action, while the other is not. Additionally, our analysis revealed the underlying reason for the 'logical circle' equivariant nature of the developed theories, encompassing a generalization of the Brown-Green-Raghunathan theorem.

Recent advancements in algebraic topology have led to significant, unsolved problems in physics that can be addressed using persistent homology, a computational tool. This method, mature after two decades of development, is now being increasingly applied across physical and mathematical sciences due to advancements in data analysis, machine learning, and descriptive topology. As a result, new applications continue to emerge. We provide an accessible introduction, including an overview of its methods and techniques, highlighting its importance and how it has already contributed significantly to physics research.

Our investigation provides a next-to-leading-order examination of $J/\psi$ angular anisotropy creation in $J/\psi$ production accompanied by an $\eta_c$ or $\chi_{cJ}$ within $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions at an energy of approximately 10.6 GeV. A detailed measurement presented by Belle in 2011 served as the foundation for our analysis. Our results, obtained via numerical assessments, indicate that next-to-leading-order contributions are essential for accurately modeling predicted $J/\psi$ angular anisotropy distributions. We found that including next-to-leading-order contributions crucially impacts the interpretation of observed $\chi_{cJ}$ production yields. Specifically, their impact greatly reduces estimated production probabilities of $\chi_{c2}$ and boosts the calculated range for $\xi_c$ in $\eta_c$ production.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who are aware of PINs and those who are not. Among those who are informed, there was limited comprehension of how PINs enhance security and user experience under various scenarios, with most perceiving PINs as an additional form of identification. Conversely, a substantial number of users doubted the necessity of PINs and expressed uncertainty about their function. Our findings suggest that users may underestimate the significance of security features, especially when such features introduce complexity, which may indicate a complementary approach is required to enhance adoption and educate users effectively.

This study presents a mathematical formula to calculate the solar properties of a surface or volume by taking into account the varying intensity of solar radiation. A weighted Gaussian quadrature rule is developed to compute the solar-weighted average of functions, and it is shown to be precise and efficient. In comparison to the standard numerical method, the quadrature rule has fewer points while achieving similar accuracy. Applications of this method are demonstrated through practical examples, including simulating solar cells and modeling molecular monolayers.

The curvature properties of a function essentially capture how different its changes are under various directions of change. Obtaining these properties is particularly challenging when evaluating functions numerically, particularly for tasks involving reinforcement learning and optimization, due to their high computational complexity. To address this issue, researchers have developed theories and methods that can accurately compute these properties using significantly fewer computations than initially thought, thus achieving a major improvement in performance time complexity.

The curvature properties are determined by the second-order derivatives of a function, also known as the Hessian matrix. Although it's often impossible to compute these derivatives due to their immense computational complexity, researchers have discovered that they can be approximated using a single training session with a deep neural network. This has led to various methods that use approximations to these derivatives to understand function behavior.

The relationship between these derivatives and a function's local changes has been understated in past research. To address this issue, researchers have developed a new method to accurately compute these derivatives while avoiding unnecessary complexity. By generalizing the Newton method's concepts, they have determined a way to accurately compute a function's changes from its training data alone. This method, also an optimization algorithm, is remarkably faster than other methods by factors of 0.01 to 0.1, thus offering a significant improvement in performance time complexity.

Beatings continue in English but are whipped away in Spanish. This contrast highlights how grammatical gender influences word associations in languages with gender specifications. Studies have shown that grammatical gender affects word associations in languages like English, but only through indirect means. However, we find a more significant impact in languages with explicit gender designations, such as French or German, where the presence of a noun's gender alters the associated concepts, particularly for nouns categorised as feminine or neutral but with feminine counterparts. This impact extends to all concept categories, and what's more, the effect is similarly strong whether the second noun has an explicit gender specification or not, indicating just how profoundly grammatical gender forces our mental image of words.

The charmability of a discrete group G refers to its ability to be embedded as a subgroup within the character group of a graph with positive spectral radius. Notably, we demonstrate that non-lattice subgroups of SL(2, ℝ) are charmable. Additionally, we establish that subgroups of SL(n, ℝ) are charmable only when they either have finite index or are isomorphic to ℝ^k for some k ≥ n. Moreover, we show that several arithmetic groups over global fields possess the charmability property. In contrast, we prove that a significant subset of unimodular arithmetic groups, including SO(n, ℝ), cannot be charmable.

Estimating an object's position has been extensively researched in both
indoor and outdoor settings but remains a challenging task, particularly for
specific categories of objects in real-world scenarios. This study addresses
this challenge by developing an approach for accurately localizing specific
categories of objects in complex environments without any prior training on
those objects. Building on a recent discovery that humans utilize environmental
 cues like doorframes and windows to establish a coordinate system, we
propose a novel method for calculating object coordinates in real-world images
by combining a deep learning model with prior knowledge of human architecture.

Recently, there has been a significant surge in demand for traffic forecasting due to various industrial and social applications, resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, among other factors. To meet this demand, researchers have developed approaches for forecasting traffic conditions on a large scale. However, existing traffic forecasting methods are typically designed with road segments having unique traffic patterns as individual units, but due to limited data availability, these methods often struggle to handle scenarios where traffic conditions vary significantly across different road segments. In response to this challenge, we propose an innovative approach called Similarity-based Attribute Extraction (SAX), which aims to improve traffic forecasting on a large scale by exploiting similar road segments with inherent traffic patterns. By applying SAX, the forecast performance is enhanced both quantitatively and substantially. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of SAX, demonstrating significantly improved forecast accuracy, with a 26.7% reduction in the root mean square error compared to baseline methods.

This study presents VACA, a new model that uses variational graph representation learning to identify relationships between multiple random variables within multiple target distributions simultaneously. By approximating random variable interactions through a learned graphical structure, VACA surpasses existing causal discovery methods by enabling the discovery of latent variables and their connections without requiring data independence or the simulation of unseen data. Furthermore, VACA facilitates the derivation of causal relationships between unobserved variables and serves as a tool for inferring counterfactual scenarios. We develop a multi-task learning approach to enhance VACA's performance, and through experiments involving both simulated and real-world data, we demonstrate that VACA effectively identifies underlying causal structures, leads to more accurate conditional causal inferences, and produces robust and sensible counterfactual predictions. The full implementation of VACA is available on the GitHub platform under the username vaca-project.

The full potential of LOFAR's real-time capabilities has yet to be seamlessly integrated into the broader scientific landscape. A groundbreaking new dataset has been collected through the continuous, 24/7 operation of the REALTA system at the Irish LOFAR station. Located at Casseymount, County Dublin, this station possesses full LOFAR functionality and has been actively collecting and processing data in real-time since 2017. Following a thorough evaluation of its system, REALTA has established a new dataset comprising approximately 25 megabytes per day, which has been actively being used to investigate various areas of astrophysical interest including radio astronomy, solar physics, and transient events in the realm of radio astronomy. Notably, it has been responsible for detecting showers and pulses of extragalactic origin, the former stemming from massive objects in the distant galaxy ARCs 16b which exhibit highly variable outflows, characterized by dish-like patterns of extreme brightness varying at times by at least one joule per square kilometer per megahertz.

Inspired by drone technology, we introduce'metaphotons' as light carriers capable of carrying information across various photonic systems at will. Leveraging cutting-edge machine learning techniques, we systematically explore the extensive realm of metaphotonics, resulting in the discovery of exceptional topological edge states that can be accessed through a single drive point to model a universal band structure. Furthermore, our findings reveal the emergence of metastable high-symmetry Dirac points within the nearly flat bulk electronic bands, as well as hybrid topological states combining type-I and type-II behavior. Notably, these extraordinary states are characterized by the presence of high propagation robustness, confinement, and chiral symmetry breaking, which can be easily regulated using a universal drive. We propose the application of metaphotonics to challenge LIGO's gravitational wave detection limits using strong laser fields, leading to the potential generation of 'drone' gravitational waves that can be detected by next-generation lunar stations.

The high-stakes business of motion pictures hinges on the prediction of box office revenue, a task made more accessible by the existence of publicly accessible movie datasets. The film industry is unique, however, due to the disparate nature of data - combining script, performance, director, and image information makes it a challenging task to construct a unified dataset. Prior research often overlooks this complexity, focusing instead on readily available attributes when predicting revenue. Our study introduces a new, more comprehensive movie dataset, leveraging a range of interesting film-related attributes, and uses it to explore the impact of these attributes on box office revenue. Our analysis, conducted across multiple machine learning model types, reveals that certain pre-defined attributes can indeed enhance revenue prediction accuracy.

The growing integration of distributed generation and storage has transformed the traditional power system dynamics, particularly the behavior of the voltage. This work examines the voltage dynamics determined by the collective response of alternative frequency control (AFC) as well as active and reactive power management. A theoretical model, the spiral dynamo, is developed to understand the characteristics of voltage fluctuations, which are then quantified using a scaling analysis inspired by the Logarithmically Circular Law. A novel metric, the Asymptotic Angular Spread, is introduced to measure system health based on the frequency of small-signal oscillations and the efficacy of AFC. Furthermore, a numerical method, the Cluster Monte Carlo, is proposed to estimate the Asymmetric Angular Spread from high-resolution active power consumption data, demonstrating its applicability to real-world power networks.

This paper centers around a tutorial session that explores cutting-edge Intelligent Networks (INs) of systems with diminished reliance on interconnected intelligent core systems. Typical networks consisting of interconnected intelligent core systems depend heavily on external intelligence, limiting the autonomy of distributed systems within the network. Distinguishing itself from conventional networks, an IN of systems, defined as an intelligent network (i-net), seeks to decrease its external intellectual dependencies by integrating embedded system intelligence that collaborates to enhance overall network robustness and efficiency in adverse environments characterized by damage or disruption. The paper presents recent advancements and discusses challenging issues related to the evaluation of robustness and efficiency in i-nets of systems, highlighting the evaluation of dependencies as a key issue. Furthermore, the paper presents a framework to assess robustness and efficiency in i-nets of systems, including scenarios and their practical applications.

Recent studies have shown that a novel method to model the inverse Compton process in relativistic electrons, taking into account polarized electron feedback, significantly altered the predicted continuum spectra using the Doppler shift and absorption model. Utilizing a Monte-Carlo approach, researchers simulated various theoretical spectra, examining a range of physical parameters including blackbody, self-similar, and broken power-law models for electrons, as well as a multi-zone scenario, to model the emission produced by electrons interacting with a target photon field. An analysis as function of energy dispersion revealed that this model, compared to previous non-polarized versions, results in a decrease or complete elimination of the UV/soft X-ray excess, to levels that could be within observational bounds, at a photon-to-radiation efficiency of approximately 10-20%. However, when considering a double-humped spectral curve, a portion of the emission in the optical to soft X-ray range can be attributed to emission produced in the Comptonization of the ambient photon field, suggesting a potential constraint on the peak energy of the emission dome in blazars, as well as providing a possible explanation for the UV/soft X-ray excess, previously attributed to emission from emission clouds, via a relativistic electron model.

Quantum field theory anomalies severely restrict the expansion of fields into complex domains near singular points, and this same set of anomalies plays a crucial role in the long-term behavior of theories within four-dimensional space-time, particularly where divergent or convergent series meet. An analytic continuation into complex domains exposes the underlying non-local structure of quantum field theories, and this exposure is especially significant in theories involving gravity where dimensionless coupling constants can take on unit values, representing boundary values between internal spaces and those encompassing the theory's outcome.

To identify whether an unknown state of a quantum system is pure or mixed, researchers use an experiment involving a single measurement. If the state is pure, a specific, non-zero value will be found with certainty. However, if the state is mixed, a range of possible values may be observed, and no single value will be found with certainty. Our study examines the scenario in which an online phase detector continuously monitors a state without interfering with its evolution, and we investigate which measurements can confirm a pure state without leaving any doubt. Specifically, our findings apply to systems comprising any number of qubits or qudits, and we identify two key categories of measurements: 'universal' observations that can confirm any pure state and'sharp' observations that can achieve the highest possible precision in measuring a pure state. Our results reveal that a measurement is both 'universal' and'sharp' if it can be found within certain entanglement-based observables, and we identify specific criteria that must be met. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that 'universal' measurements are, in fact,'sharp', and we discuss the practical implications for implementing these measurements in experiments.

Baryon and meson masses have been calculated using a quantum fragmentation model based on light-cone QCD strings. The model quantitatively describes baryon and meson mass distributions. The prediction of the baryon masses is accurate to the level of 10 percent, while meson masses have an even lower percentage error. The model successfully accounts for the masses of particles composed from various types of quarks, and reveals a common mass pattern that applies universally.

The study aimed to understand how solar surface disturbances, particularly those associated with active regions, influence north-south helioseismic travel-time measurements. To achieve this, it used a simulation based on the MFLOOST code to model surface flows resulting from buoyant updrafts and also took into account the impact of surface currents resulting from these uplifts. The research analyzed how these surface currents affect travel-time measurements in different directions and found a significant correlation between the orientation of active regions and the travel-time measurements. Specifically, it observed a delay in travel-time measurements for observations made in the same direction as the active region and an acceleration for those made in the opposite direction. The study used results from the SOHO/MDI to validate its findings and provided insights into how to interpret and refine travel-time measurements in relation to active regions.

This research examines the potential gravitational waves in the frequency range of 1-100 nHz, measured by pulsars, to determine if they could originate from the early universe. A low-frequency gravitational wave detector such as the Pulsar Timing Array is sensitive to the early universe and its long-wavelength, large-scale magnetic fields. For example, if the primordial magnetic fields have a hierarchy of scales similar to our current understanding, its power spectrum would decrease at lower frequencies, which in turn could produce anisotropic gravitational waves in the same frequency range. A specific type of magnetic field with this characteristic can produce a quadrupole moment, resulting in irreversible gravitational waves. Assuming the early universe had similar anisotropies on large scales, the analysis concludes that the intergalactic magnetic fields could produce significant gravitational waves, approximately 1-100 fM, which is comparable to the LISA's sensitivity to individual sources, making it a potential detectable phenomenon with the PTN and future instruments like the NANOGrav and SKA.

Large-scale light-field displays can produce the most immersive visual experiences, but advancements in home entertainment technologies are hindered by limitations in compressing and efficiently encoding light fields. We introduce PLF-Net, a novel light-field compression model, which uniquely accounts for the effects of parallax when encoding images. Unlike traditional methods that only optimize encoded data, our proposed system also optimizes the modulation domain through an adaptive configuration process. This allows PLF-Net to yield significant compression performance improvements, with results showing it outperforms existing approaches by a substantial margin, with an average 78.27% improvement in PSNR values and 73.22% improvement in SSIM values, all while maintaining a comparable encoding bit count.

The goal of Cross-Lingual Information Retrieval is to enable search engines to identify a user's query a relevant document, even if the query is in a language the system doesn't understand. To achieve this, researchers use machine learning models that can translate the query into a known language and rely on a pre-trained model, often based on embeddings, to rank documents based on their relevance. There are two types of models used in this context: interactive models that learn to predict a score based on an embedded query and a document, and non-interactive models that can translate queries and generate document embeddings using a pre-defined set of parameters. To improve the overall performance of this retrieval task, this paper proposes combining the benefits of interactive and non-interactive models in a modular approach, where the proposal of non-interactive models is refined by interactive models to produce the final ranked list. To accomplish this, the researchers introduce a novel architecture that can translate the query, map the query and the document to a common space, and predict a score, all while sharing and optimizing parameters efficiently. The experiments conducted on three datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach over non-interactive models and highlight its effectiveness in retrieving top-ranked results. Additionally, the researchers analyze the performance of the proposed model and demonstrate its robustness to language complexity, while showing room for further improvement in retrieving lower-ranked results.

The importance of accurate demographic and health statistics cannot be overstated, particularly in rural areas where many low-income nations are struggling with growing health issues. To effectively track these developments, administrators need reliable tools for monitoring population health and key indicators such as fertility rates, despite a lack of comprehensive individual data. Instead, officials rely on aggregate information from small-scale geographic areas. Therefore, administrators utilize area-based data combined with additional information sources, employing statistical techniques known as small-area estimation to generate more precise estimates. Two prominent approaches used in this process are design-based and model-based estimation methods, with a long-standing debate surrounding their comparative validity. To compare these methods, researchers typically rely on simulated data, making real-world testing a rare occurrence where actual data is available. This study examines fertility rate estimates in rural Kenya, using survey data from women who reported their village, district, and county of residence, providing a unique opportunity to assess small-area estimation techniques in a real-world setting. By considering two critical factors as effect modifiers - education and access to a healthcare system - both design- and model-based estimators were analyzed, with feedforward neural networks, lasso, and Bayesian additive regression tree models utilized as features to build models. It was discovered that both design- and model-based estimators, particularly those that accounted for education, yielded remarkably accurate results, with model-based estimators offering more consistency and fewer extreme outcomes. Notably, incorporating education as a factor produced the most accurate estimates, with similar results found when

This research introduces a novel betting strategy inspired by Kelly's work and applies it to a quantum-scale casino. By allowing players to place bets on quantum states within a defined space, with the casino offering a mixture of money and quantum states as rewards, a method for determining optimal bet sizes is established. A possible implementation based on optical systems is also described.

Recently, researchers discovered new potential p-type chalcogenide topological insulators in the MA$_2$Z$_4$ structure. To assess the potential of MA$_2$Z$_4$ as electronic or optoelectronic devices, we utilize computational methods to investigate their band arrangements. Our analysis covers 16 variations of MA$_2$Z$_4$, created by combining different elements, and focuses on the band arrangements resulting from substituting atoms. We identify four distinct types of band arrangements in these variations: type I, characterized by type-II Dirac points in the valence band, type II, featuring large gapless bands, type X, associated with an exotic $D_{3h}$ symmetry, and type N, marked by nodal lines; and six non-BAND structures. In the type I, type II, and type X variations, we observe significant quasiparticle corrections that result in new band arrangements called type I$, type II$ and type X$. Notably, the electron occupation per band in the type I, type II, and type X variations matches the count of the stacking layers, suggesting that multiple conjugated transitions contribute to these band arrangements. Furthermore, the electron occupation per band in the type I$, type II$ and type X variations is one, indicating the dominance of a single conjugated transition, and predicts that MA$_2$Z$_4$ could display unique characteristics under tension or compression, such as stretching the stacking layers to vary

A new search for the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay is reported, using data collected by the LHCb experiment at the LHC. The observed branching fraction is $1.23 \pm 0.29 \pm 0.24 \times 10^{-8}$. This result is based on $3.0 \pm 0.3 \,\rm fb^{-1}$ of data, and is consistent with a prior study. Combining this with other evidence, scientists have refined their understanding of the $\Sigma^+ \mu^+ \mu^- $ channel, and have set new limits on several theoretical models, including the West and Chikovski and Grinstein theories. The LHCb data is the first to detect this decay, and it provides the most accurate measurement of its branching fraction to date.

A widely accepted theory is that the formation of protoplanetary disks occurs when a prestellar core collapses, yet it's unclear how the core's material transforms into the observed disk properties. Our study presents a model for this transformation, which involves high-speed shocks to reveal the dynamics of core collapse and disk development. When a prestellar core initially collapses, its center undergoes a slow, outer radial movement due to gravitational instability, while outer layers create a filament oriented along the rotation axis, stored with kinetic energy. As mass builds up at the center, the filament's leading edge gains speed, typically around 0.1-1 km/s, and when it overtake's the center, a highly energetic and extended shock forms, spanning tens of astronomical units. This shock causes a significant outburst of gas, which then spreads into a vast shell, expanding at about 1-3 km/s, and fills the surrounding volume with gas. As shock waves continue to form at the edge of this expanding shell, they create new, smaller shocks with lower energies, which propagate inward and cause local pressure increases that help stop the gas flow towards the center. As a result, an outer disk with an inner cut-off forms, which eventually shrinks in size over time. Our model also suggests that the inner disk formation is not instantaneous but rather occurs in stages due to the collapse of smaller, residual clouds, which creates the observed spectral energy distributions and mass accretion rates for young stars.

A comprehensive study on atmospheric dispersion, conducted across various elevations in France, revealed a notable dependence of atmospheric dispersion on altitude, which cannot be replicated by existing models. Consequently, a novel set of parametric models has been developed to accurately capture the atmospheric dispersion behavior across a wide range of altitudes from 350 to 1000 meters above sea level. This new model is presented in detail, and it efficiently predicts atmospheric dispersion for telescope installations above sea level for all wavelengths, except in the vicinity of water vapor bands. Moreover, this model has been successfully applied to correct telescope aperture losses resulting from atmospheric dispersion, thereby enabling precise photometric measurements to be achieved.

We utilize the probabilistic framework of GRUVAR, an extension of the GRU model through variational inference, to tackle the issue of sparse multi-period forecasting in data series. Our approach, GRUVAR, offers improved expressive power with the ability to capture complex temporal relationships and learn efficient, variational approximations tailored to each time step's predictions, thereby reducing redundancy. We apply a Bayesian framework to represent the model parameters as latent functions and impose sparsity via Poisson process-based regularization. Our novel method, GRUVAR, outperforms state-of-the-art state-space and deep learning methods in multi-step forecasting tasks.

In a setting that combines model theory and algebraic geometry, we establish a link between Stone duality and Pontryagin duality through the lens of constant logic. This connection implies that a compact abelian group's dual can be represented as a Bohr space, which in turn corresponds to a constant logic formula's interpretation within an ultrapower of the real numbers. This relationship has practical consequences, demonstrating that a Bohr space's topology can be captured using first-order logic, specifically constant logic.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding its ethical implications. Two main areas of expertise, fairness in statistical analysis and differential privacy, are actively developing their own models and methodologies. Notably, the framework of quantized federated learning not only enhances the model's security but also adheres to the principles of differential privacy. This work will explore the intersection of these three areas of study, revealing how they interact and form cross connections that will be supported by a thoroughly detailed, technical presentation.

In a supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model, a straightforward $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry can be introduced with two new gauginos that can contribute to dark energy due to their very low mass, which can be established by incorporating a hidden $Z'$ boson into the theory. However, the introduction of these new particles must be consistent with existing experimental data on supersymmetry and dark matter. Therefore, the focus is on creating a model in which the $U(1)_X$ symmetry can efficiently transfer momentum to the hidden sector, leading to a proper dark matter behavior without violating experimental bounds on the $Z'$ boson mass. This model can be established within the mSUGRA framework by setting the $Z'$ mass equal to 700 GeV and the $U(1)_X$ coupling to 0.1, resulting in the correct dark matter abundance with an appropriate relic density. Furthermore, the model can be made to behave correctly in terms of neutrino mixing and the invisible higgsino decays to the $U(1)_X$ gauge boson without affecting its higgsino dark matter production at the LHC.

We investigate how to improve the performance of a wireless-powered network assisted by an intelligent surface, even when there's interference from the transmitter to the receiver. To this end, we develop a method for optimizing the electromagnetic surface's phase shifts over time. Initially, we frame this problem as a convex optimization task using data from the network's initial stage, but this approach has limitations due to the need for prior knowledge of certain parameters. Therefore, we propose an artificial neural network solution that can learn from data without this limitation, using a dataset generated from the problem's constraints. Our results show that this approach can effectively solve the optimization task and can also be used for other problems in communications.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, along with the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by utilizing a combination of two-component RPA theories that considers both protons and neutrons as the primary excitation sources. The calculated and measured beta decay distributions align when considering the varying complexities of the two-component RPE and experimental error margins, respectively. The calculated half-life for $^{186}$Hg is now accurately described with a measured half-life of $18.175\pm0.008$ seconds, indicating a measured Gamow-Teller strength of $6.682\pm0.015$ units and a calculated QRPA strength of $7.959$, in agreement within one-standard deviation.

Within the framework of Sube-sube Sube-sube (3-3-3) model, the anomaly of substance dark matter is attributed to a dark gauge theory, proposed to also influence the nature of neutrinas, thereby indicating neutrino nature through dark gauge hidden sector. This early dark sector particle has been found to significantly impact baryogenesis and leptogenesis processes. Research has shown that successful baryogenesis and leptogenesis heavily rely on the dark gauge hidden sector. Specifically, the dark Higgs mediation in the neutrino mass matrix yields a sufficient condition for both baryogenesis and leptogenesis, thereby indicating that the dark sector has a substantial influence on these processes. This 3-3-3 model serves as a distinct framework for understanding the relationship between dark matter, baryogenesis, and leptogenesis processes.

We have recently found that robots can learn diverse skills using simulated data, side information, and a few real system parameters. A new learning approach called End-to-End Goal-Oriented Skill Learning (EEGOS) iteratively develops a range of skills by creating a series of targets defined by a natural equation representing desired system behavior. Unlike conventional methods, EEGOS achieves skill generalization without needing numerous demonstrations, even with only partial information on the dynamics, by leveraging informative parameters derived from side information. We show that by adjusting these parameters, the target equation can generate various skills, such as flying and swimming, which are inherently connected. Moreover, our EEGOS method converges rapidly because it utilizes an online prediction method that reduces the need for extensive online learning. We validate the effectiveness of EEGOS by having it successfully train a flying, swimming, walking, and jumping quadrotor without any real-world data, using only readily available parameters as guides.

In the context of the Sl3 Toda conformal field theory, specifically for Toda characters associated with irreducible modules of the Uq[sl3, L)] algebra, a mathematical framework is established to derive Ward relationships among these characters. This, in turn, provides an alternative method for describing the characteristics of modules within Toda conformal field theory. Additionally, this developed approach is shown to have explicit applications in calculating partition functions for soliton solutions of the Toda molecular crystal Hamiltonian. It is found that specific soliton configurations give rise to partition functions that are classically equivalent to Fermi gas free fermion systems. Moreover, in the semi-classical limit, these Toda partition functions are shown to adhere to Ward relationships. Conversely, in the Toda framework, these Ward relationships can be used to express the partition functions of any soliton configuration in an alternate form. It is found that for any number of solitons, Toda partition functions exhibit symmetrical properties and can be expressed in terms of Uq[sl3, L)] character. This includes examples involving up to five solitons. Furthermore, in the Toda framework, the Uq[sl3, L)] character of specific Toda solutions exhibit semi-classical behaviors that are classically equivalent to those of the Fermi gas free fermion system. This includes examples of two, three, four, and five free fermions.

The effectiveness of Relation Networks (RNs) in GANs depends on the type of loss function used, with metrics like Frechet Inception Distance (FID) and Intersection over Union (IoU) being influential factors, albeit to a limited extent. By incorporating a more comprehensive set of metrics including triplet loss, including one-to-one and one-to-many mappings, we have developed a novel architecture, RN-GAN. This model leverages RNs to learn data and approximation distributions, improving the quality of generated images, while also increasing diversity, as measured by FID and IoU scores. Moreover, RN-GAN has been shown to yield superior performance, surpassing state-of-the-art results, with a notable margin of 2.35 and 3.21 in FID and IoU scores, respectively.

We have successfully implemented a new method for non-secure communication in quantum key exchange without relying on the locking of phase patterns. By introducing a distinct method for managing interference patterns, we have been able to achieve reliable key distribution results with an average error rate of under 7% and an average fidelity of around 67% within a single experimental setting, outperforming previous approaches, including those involving locked phase patterns, which achieved a maximum of 40% fidelity. This breakthrough enables the integration of an error correction step into the process of secure quantum key exchange, while also enabling the exchange of secure keys through a conditional application of rotation. Notably, we have demonstrated the exchange of multiple secure keys subsequent to each other, with a maximum of 20 key settings, despite the exchange taking place without the locking of phase patterns. This new method also allows for the exchange of secure keys at a relatively fast rate, with an average duration of around 3.6 seconds to achieve 10 key settings, making it an important development in the field of quantum key exchange.
